blocks.text:
Depression leaves a person with no drive. Sure, being bullied at school is cruel, sure, domestic violence is cruel, but at least there should be a little drive left to live normally, right? To keep yourself from one day starving to death and being cursed as 'that dumbass is just plain lazy!', here comes Zoloft.
Sertraline~ Sertraline~ You're my Rescuer~

SRI is serotonin reuptake inhibition. SSRI is selective serotonin reuptake inhibition, a subset of SRI; SNRI inhibits the reuptake of both serotonin and noradrenaline. All of them are antidepressants and anxiolytics, not 'happy pills'.
Mechanism: Slow the Recycling Down
After a nerve cell releases serotonin, it takes it back up through a transporter. SRI inhibits that reuptake, so serotonin stays longer in the synaptic cleft.

But this doesn't make a person happy right away. The receptors need time to adapt, and the antidepressant effect usually takes a few weeks; during those weeks the side effects tend to arrive first and the benefit later. That's the black humour in the line 'here comes Zoloft': it does come, just very slowly.
Effects

items: Main side effects: sexual inhibition, SSRI withdrawal, insomnia or drowsiness, nausea, sweating.
Acute side effects: serotonin syndrome, sexual inhibition, anxiety.

blocks.text: The source text's precautions consisted of one sentence: 'Sertraline can't be o'd.' That isn't a moral judgment but a pharmacological one: an SSRI overdose won't give you the 'high' you want, but will push serotonin to a dangerous place.
The Five Golden Flowers

The circle calls the classic SSRIs the 'five golden flowers': fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, fluvoxamine, citalopram/escitalopram. Their mechanisms are similar; they differ mainly in metabolism speed, degree of sedation and withdrawal reactions.

In ODW's cards, 'five golden flowers' is no longer one card but the collective name of five SSRI cards: fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, fluvoxamine, citalopram. All five carry the 'five golden flowers' tag and all stack a layer of serotonin load; the specific effects differ slightly (delay, sedation, withdrawal, stacking with dextro in the same round). Take sertraline: mind +5, +3 two rounds later, serotonin load +1.
Serotonin Syndrome

When there's too much serotonin, a person gets fever, sweating, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, altered consciousness and a racing heart; in severe cases it can be fatal. This isn't 'the effect being too strong', it's the system going beyond its regulatory range.

Stack two serotonergic drugs and the risk isn't additive, it's multiplicative. Dextromethorphan itself has SRI action; stacked with an SSRI, it's a common combination for serotonin syndrome. The source text left only one cautious reminder about combining dextro with antidepressants and gave no protocol — this piece won't give one either.
Withdrawal

SSRIs need to be tapered down slowly, dose by dose. After a sudden stop there can be dizziness, nausea, anxiety, insomnia, electric-shock sensations; these symptoms disguise themselves as 'the illness coming back', making people think they can't stop.
Recovery technique files it under 'discontinuation reaction': not a new illness, just a withdrawal that happened too fast.
It Isn't a Stimulant
The specific entries separate 'stimulation' from 'antidepressant' very clearly:
Stimulation lifts normal to high; antidepressant lifts low to high.

An SSRI pulls a low person back to normal, and won't push a normal person toward high. So it shouldn't be used as a stimulant; for someone without depression it brings mostly side effects rather than happiness.
Closing
It pulls a low person back to normal, but it won't push a normal person toward high.
